input.name: nums and target
input.description: A strictly increasing array was rotated, and we must find target 1 in logarithmic time.

explanation.intuition: Although the whole array is not sorted after rotation, at least one half around every midpoint is still sorted. By identifying that sorted half, we can tell whether the target could lie inside it; if not, we discard it and continue in the other half.
approach: Start with left pointer l at index 0 and right pointer r at the final index.
Compute the middle index mid of the current search range.
If nums[mid] equals the target, return mid immediately.
Check whether the left half from l through mid is sorted.
If the left half is sorted, keep it only when the target lies between nums[l] and nums[mid]; otherwise search the right half.
If the left half is not sorted, the right half must be sorted. Keep or discard that half using the same range test.
Repeat until the target is found or l moves beyond r.
explanation.whyItWorks: Because all values are unique, each midpoint divides the current range into one sorted half and one possibly rotated half. The target can be ruled out of the sorted half exactly when it is outside that half's numeric range, so each update discards a half that cannot contain the target. Therefore, if the target exists it remains in the search range until it is found.
pitfalls: Use l <= r rather than l < r, because a final one-element range must still be checked.
The comparisons use <= when deciding whether the left portion is sorted; this also correctly handles a one-element left portion.
Do not use ordinary binary-search comparisons alone, because the full rotated array is not globally sorted.
This version assumes all elements are unique. With duplicates, nums[l] == nums[mid] can make the sorted side ambiguous.
In languages where indexes can be very large, compute the midpoint as l + (r - l) / 2 to avoid overflow.

steps.description: The search begins on nums = [3, 4, 5, 6, 1, 2], with target 1. We set l to 0 and r to 5 so the initial search range includes every array position; no answer has been found yet.
The current range runs from index 0 through index 5, so it contains all six values. Since 0 <= 5 is true, the while loop enters its first iteration and the target may still be present.
The middle of the active range from 0 to 5 is index 2, where nums[2] is 5. This midpoint splits the current range into a left part and a right part that we can reason about.
The midpoint value is nums[2] = 5, while the target is 1. Because 1 is not equal to 5, the function cannot return index 2 and must determine which half can contain 1.

We compare the endpoints of the left half: nums[0] = 3 and nums[2] = 5. Since 3 <= 5, indices 0 through 2 form the sorted portion [3, 4, 5], so we can test whether target 1 belongs in that numeric interval.

The first condition for excluding the sorted left half asks whether target 1 is greater than nums[2] = 5. Since 1 > 5 is false, C++ must evaluate the second part of the OR condition before choosing a direction.
steps.calculation:
target > nums[mid]
1 > 5  ->  false
false || (...) requires evaluating the second comparison

steps.description: The second condition compares target 1 with the left endpoint nums[0] = 3. Because 1 < 3 is true, 1 cannot occur in the sorted values [3, 4, 5], so the algorithm must discard that entire left half.
steps.calculation:
target < nums[l]
1 < nums[0] = 3  ->  true
false || true  ->  true

steps.description: The target is outside the sorted interval from 3 through 5, so indices 0, 1, and 2 cannot contain it. We move l from 0 to mid + 1 = 3, preserving only indices 3 through 5 where the target could still appear.
The remaining search range starts at index 3 and ends at index 5, containing [6, 1, 2]. Since 3 <= 5 is true, there are still candidates to inspect and the loop begins another iteration.
The middle of the remaining range from index 3 to index 5 is index 4. At that position nums[4] = 1, which is the value we need to compare with the target.
The midpoint value nums[4] = 1 exactly matches target 1. The equality test succeeds, so index 4 is confirmed as the target's location and no more halves need to be examined.
Because the target 1 was found at midpoint index 4, the function returns 4 immediately. This is correct because nums[4] = 1, and all earlier discarded ranges were proven unable to contain the target.

visualization.title: Search in a Rotated Sorted Array
visualization.algorithm: Find rotation pivot, then binary search each sorted segment

input.name: nums and target
input.description: The array was sorted ascending and then rotated; every value is unique.

explanation.intuition: A rotated sorted array has one special location: the smallest value, called the pivot. Everything before that location is sorted, and everything from that location to the end is also sorted. We can locate the pivot with binary search by comparing the middle value with the rightmost value, then use ordinary binary search on each sorted portion.
approach: Start with pointers at both ends of the array.
Repeatedly inspect the middle value and compare it with the rightmost value.
If the middle value is larger than the rightmost value, the smallest value must be to the middle's right; otherwise it is at or to the middle's left.
When the pointers meet, that index is the pivot, or smallest value.
Binary-search the sorted segment before the pivot.
If the target is absent there, binary-search the sorted segment beginning at the pivot.
explanation.whyItWorks: At every pivot-search iteration, the smallest value remains inside the interval from l through r. A middle value larger than nums[r] lies in the left, larger sorted run, so the pivot must be after it. Otherwise the middle is in the right run or is itself the pivot, so the pivot cannot be after it. Once the pivot splits the array into two normally sorted ranges, ordinary binary search correctly finds the target if it exists.
pitfalls: The pivot loop uses l < r, not l <= r, because it stops when one possible pivot index remains.
The ordinary binary-search loop uses left <= right so that a one-element range is checked.
This version relies on unique values; duplicates make nums[m] == nums[r] ambiguous during pivot detection.
If the array is not rotated, the pivot is index 0 and the first binary-search range is empty.
For extremely large indices in C++, use left + (right - left) / 2 to avoid possible integer overflow.

steps.description: We begin search(nums, 1) with the rotated array [3, 4, 5, 6, 1, 2]. The goal is to first locate the smallest value, which will split the array into two sorted ranges for the final search.

The pivot search starts over the entire six-element array, so l becomes 0 and r becomes 5. These pointers enclose every index that could still contain the smallest value; no answer has been found yet.
The current pivot interval runs from index 0 through index 5, so it contains more than one candidate. Because 0 < 5 is true, the loop continues and will inspect a middle position.
The middle of indices 0 and 5 is index 2, whose value is 5. This value will tell us which side of the rotation boundary still contains the smallest element.
nums[2] is 5 while the rightmost value nums[5] is 2. Since 5 > 2, index 2 is in the larger left run, so the smallest value and pivot must lie strictly to its right.
Because the pivot cannot be at index 2 or anywhere before it, l moves to index 3. The remaining possible pivot interval is now indices 3 through 5, while the final answer is still unknown.
The narrowed pivot interval is from index 3 to index 5, and it still has multiple candidates. Since 3 < 5 is true, another middle value must be examined.
The middle of the current interval [3, 5] is index 4, containing value 1. Comparing this value to the interval's right edge determines whether the pivot is at or before this middle index.
nums[4] is 1 and nums[5] is 2, so the middle value is not larger than the rightmost value. That means index 4 is already in the right sorted run, and the pivot is at index 4 or somewhere to its left.
The pivot remains possible at index 4, so r is moved directly to the middle index rather than past it. The candidate interval becomes indices 3 through 4, and the answer is still being searched for.
Indices 3 and 4 are still different, so there are two possible pivot locations remaining. Because 3 < 4 is true, the pivot loop performs one more middle comparison.
The middle of indices 3 and 4 is index 3 because integer division discards the fractional part. nums[3] is 6, and this is the final value needed to isolate the rotation point.
nums[3] is 6, which is greater than nums[4], which is 1. Therefore index 3 is still in the left sorted run, and the smallest value must be immediately after it.
Since the pivot is strictly right of index 3, l advances to index 4. Both boundaries now meet at the only remaining pivot candidate, which is value 1.
The two pivot boundaries meet at index 4, so there is exactly one candidate remaining. Since 4 < 4 is false, the loop stops and confirms that this location is the pivot.
The pivot is assigned from l, so pivot becomes index 4 where the smallest value 1 begins. This divides the array into sorted ranges [3, 4, 5, 6] and [1, 2] for ordinary binary searches.

The first binarySearch call examines the sorted range before the pivot, from index 0 through index 3. Its local bounds become left = 0 and right = 3; target 1 is not yet known to be absent or present.
The first binary-search range from index 0 to index 3 is nonempty. Because 0 <= 3 is true, the helper will calculate and inspect its middle index.
The middle of the sorted range [0, 3] is index 1, whose value is 4. We now compare 4 with the target 1 to decide which half can still contain the target.
The inspected value nums[1] is 4, not the target 1. Equality fails, so this call cannot return index 1 and must determine whether 1 belongs to a smaller or larger half.
Value 4 is also not less than target 1, so the target would have to be on the smaller left side of index 1. The helper will discard index 1 and every larger index in this sorted range.
Since nums[1] = 4 is greater than target 1, right moves left to index 0. Only nums[0] = 3 remains to be checked in this first sorted segment.
The remaining first-range interval contains exactly index 0, so it must still be checked. Because 0 <= 0 is true, binary search evaluates this last possible value.
With left and right both at 0, the middle is index 0 and its value is 3. This is the final candidate in the array portion before the pivot.
nums[0] equals 3, while the target remains 1, so this candidate is not a match. The helper continues to its less-than comparison to choose the only possible direction.
The value 3 is greater than 1, so nums[0] is not less than the target. Since this sorted range has no values further left, its search interval will become empty.
Because nums[0] = 3 is larger than target 1, right moves to -1. This places right before left, proving that target 1 does not occur in indices 0 through 3.
The first binary-search interval is empty because left is 0 but right is -1. Since 0 <= -1 is false, the helper has exhausted the left sorted segment without finding target 1.
The first binarySearch call returns -1 because none of its examined values 4 and 3 matched target 1. This only rules out the segment before the pivot; the pivot segment still may contain the answer.

The returned value -1 is assigned to result, recording that target 1 was absent from indices 0 through 3. The outer method will now test this result before deciding whether to search the second sorted segment.
The condition checks whether the first search found a valid index, but result is -1. Since -1 != -1 is false, the method does not return yet and must search from the pivot onward.
The final return statement calls binarySearch on the sorted pivot segment from index 4 through index 5. Its local bounds are left = 4 and right = 5, covering values [1, 2] where target 1 may appear.
The second binary-search range from index 4 to index 5 contains two values and is nonempty. Because 4 <= 5 is true, the helper computes a middle index to test target 1.
The middle of indices 4 and 5 is index 4 after integer division. nums[4] is 1, so this first probe in the pivot segment can be compared directly with target 1.
The middle value nums[4] is exactly 1, which matches the target 1. The second binary search has found the target's index, so it immediately returns index 4.
The helper returns mid, which is index 4, because nums[4] equals target 1. This valid index becomes the value returned by the outer search method's final return statement.
The outer search returns index 4, and nums[4] is indeed the target value 1. The pivot split allowed both sorted segments to be searched logarithmically, so the final answer is 4.
